title: Course Schedule II
directAnswer: Model courses as a directed graph where an edge b → a means 'b is a prerequisite of a'. A valid order is a topological sort. The canonical answer is Kahn's algorithm (BFS): compute every node's in-degree, start a queue with the zero-in-degree nodes, and repeatedly pop a node into the output while decrementing its neighbours' in-degrees, enqueuing any that hit zero. If you output fewer than numCourses nodes, the graph has a cycle → return []. O(V + E) time. DFS post-order reversal is the equivalent alternative.

remember.pattern: Topological sort of a DAG (Kahn's BFS or DFS post-order)
rules: Edge direction is **prerequisite → course**: `[a, b]` means take `b` before `a`, so add edge `b → a` and `indegree[a]++`.
Start Kahn's queue with **every** zero-in-degree node, not just node 0.
Append a node to the output the moment you **pop** it (its prerequisites are already placed).
If the final order has **fewer than numCourses** nodes, a cycle exists → return an **empty array**.
DFS variant: push each node in **post-order**, then **reverse**; a back-edge to a node still on the recursion stack is a cycle.
whenToUse: Ordering tasks/courses under 'X must come before Y' dependency constraints
Build systems, package install order, spreadsheet recalculation order
Detecting whether a dependency graph is acyclic AND producing a valid sequence
Any DAG where you need a linear order respecting all directed edges
antiSignals: You only need a yes/no 'is it possible?' → Course Schedule I (cycle detection alone)
Edges are undirected → connectivity / spanning tree, not topo sort
You need the SHORTEST path or longest chain → BFS/DP on the DAG, not just any topo order
remember.takeaway: Course Schedule II is the canonical topological-sort problem. Kahn's algorithm gives you ordering and cycle detection in one pass; DFS post-order is the same result from the other direction. Master both and you've unlocked Alien Dictionary, Parallel Courses, and build-dependency questions.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise a dependency-ordering problem as a topological sort, build the graph with the correct edge direction, and handle the cycle case by returning an empty array rather than a partial order.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Reversing the edge direction (so the order comes out backwards), forgetting that a cycle must return [], or only seeding the queue with node 0 instead of all zero-in-degree nodes.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name it as topological sort immediately, explain Kahn's in-degree intuition, show that 'output size < n ⇒ cycle' is free cycle detection, and mention the DFS post-order alternative and where each is preferable.

problemStatement:
There are a total of `numCourses` courses you have to take, labeled from `0` to `numCourses - 1`. You are given an array `prerequisites` where `prerequisites[i] = [aᵢ, bᵢ]` indicates that you **must take course `bᵢ` first** if you want to take course `aᵢ`.

Return *the ordering of courses you should take to finish all courses*. If there are many valid answers, return **any** of them. If it is impossible to finish all courses, return **an empty array**.
constraints: All the pairs [aᵢ, bᵢ] are distinct
understanding: We need a linear ordering of all courses such that every prerequisite appears before the course that needs it. That's exactly a topological sort of the directed prerequisite graph. If the graph contains a cycle, no valid ordering exists and we return an empty array.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which direction does [a, b] point — does a depend on b or b on a?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: [a, b] means b is a prerequisite of a, so b must come first. I'll add a directed edge b → a and increment a's in-degree.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What do I return if the courses can't all be finished?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: An empty array. That happens exactly when the graph has a cycle, which my algorithm detects when the output is shorter than numCourses.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can there be multiple valid orderings?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — any valid topological order is accepted. The order among independent (zero-in-degree) courses is arbitrary.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can prerequisites be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. With no edges every course has in-degree 0, so any permutation (e.g. 0,1,2,…) is valid.

examples.explanation: Course 1 depends on course 0, so 0 must come first → [0, 1].
0 has no prerequisites. Both 1 and 2 need 0; 3 needs both 1 and 2. [0,2,1,3] is also valid — the order of 1 and 2 is interchangeable.
0 needs 1 and 1 needs 0 — a cycle. No valid ordering exists, so return an empty array.

approaches.name: Kahn's Algorithm — BFS Topological Sort (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. Phrase it as 'repeatedly take any course whose prerequisites are all already scheduled' — that's the in-degree-zero frontier.
hints: A course can be taken once all its prerequisites are done. In graph terms, that's a node whose in-degree (number of incoming prerequisite edges) has dropped to zero.
Compute every node's in-degree, then start a queue with all zero-in-degree nodes. Pop one into the answer, and 'finish' it by decrementing each neighbour's in-degree.
When a neighbour's in-degree hits zero, all its prerequisites are scheduled — enqueue it. If you end up scheduling fewer than numCourses nodes, the leftover nodes form a cycle → return [].
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the graph touches every edge once → O(E). Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once → O(V), and across all dequeues we examine each outgoing edge once more → O(E). Total O(V + E) time; the adjacency list and in-degree array are O(V + E) space.
approaches.explanation:
Kahn's algorithm builds the schedule the way a student actually would: at any moment, take any course whose prerequisites are *all* already behind you.

**In-degree is the readiness counter.** For each course we count how many prerequisites point into it — that's its in-degree. A course with in-degree 0 has nothing blocking it, so it's immediately takeable. We seed the queue with *every* such course, because in general there can be many independent starting points, not just course 0. (Seeding only node 0 is a classic bug that breaks the moment two courses have no prerequisites.)

**Finishing a course unblocks its dependents.** When we pop a course `u` and append it to the order, we've 'completed' it. Every course `v` that listed `u` as a prerequisite now has one fewer thing blocking it, so we decrement `indegree[v]`. The instant `indegree[v]` reaches 0, *all* of `v`'s prerequisites are scheduled, so `v` becomes takeable and we enqueue it. This ripple is what propagates the ordering outward from the roots.

**Why the edge direction is prerequisite → course.** The input `[a, b]` says 'take `b` before `a`'. So `b` enables `a`: the edge runs `b → a`, and it's `a` whose in-degree goes up. Getting this backwards produces a perfectly valid topological order of the *reversed* graph — which is exactly the wrong answer. State the direction out loud before you wire up the adjacency list.

**Cycle detection comes for free.** In a DAG every node eventually reaches in-degree 0 and gets scheduled, so the output has all `numCourses` nodes. But if there's a cycle, the nodes on that cycle perpetually block each other — none of them ever reaches in-degree 0, so they're never enqueued. The output ends up *shorter* than `numCourses`, and that single length check (`order.size != numCourses`) is all the cycle detection we need. Return an empty array in that case.
approaches.insight: Kahn's algorithm is really 'peeling the graph from its sources'. The in-degree array is a set of countdown timers; finishing a node ticks down its successors, and a node fires the moment its timer hits zero. The leftover nodes that never fire are precisely the cycle — so ordering and cycle detection fall out of the same loop.

code.python:
from collections import deque

def findOrder(self, numCourses: int, prerequisites: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
    adj = [[] for _ in range(numCourses)]
    indegree = [0] * numCourses
    for course, prereq in prerequisites:
        adj[prereq].append(course)  # edge: prerequisite -> course
        indegree[course] += 1

    queue = deque(i for i in range(numCourses) if indegree[i] == 0)
    order = []
    while queue:
        course = queue.popleft()
        order.append(course)
        for nxt in adj[course]:
            indegree[nxt] -= 1
            if indegree[nxt] == 0:
                queue.append(nxt)

    return order if len(order) == numCourses else []

The course (p[0]) gains an incoming prerequisite, so its readiness counter rises.
Seed the queue with EVERY zero-prerequisite course, not just course 0.
Finishing 'course' unblocks 'next'; when its last prerequisite clears, it becomes takeable.

pitfalls: Reversing the edge direction — produces a valid order of the reversed graph (i.e. wrong answer).
Seeding the queue with only node 0 instead of all zero-in-degree nodes.
Returning the partial order on a cycle instead of an empty array.
Using a list with pop(0) as the queue — O(n) per pop; use a deque/LinkedList.

approaches.name: DFS Post-Order with 3-Color Cycle Detection
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as the recursive equivalent. Useful when you already think in DFS, or want to reuse the same cycle-check from Course Schedule I.
hints: Topological order is the reverse of DFS finish times. So DFS the whole graph, push each node when you finish exploring all its descendants, then reverse the list.
To detect cycles, colour each node white (unvisited), grey (on the current recursion stack), or black (fully done).
If DFS ever reaches a grey node, you've looped back onto the current path — that's a cycle, so bail out and return [].
approaches.complexityReasoning: DFS visits every node once (guarded by the colour state) and traverses every edge once → O(V + E). The recursion stack and the colour/order arrays are O(V + E) space.
approaches.explanation:
DFS produces a topological order from the opposite end: instead of emitting sources first, it emits *sinks* first and reverses.

**Finish order is reverse topological order.** When a DFS from node `u` returns, every node reachable from `u` has already been fully explored and pushed. So if we append `u` *after* recursing into all its neighbours (post-order), the nodes with no outstanding dependents land earliest in the list. Appending in post-order and then reversing yields a valid topological order — every prerequisite ends up before the course that needs it.

**The three colours encode recursion state.** White means 'not yet visited'. Grey means 'currently on the recursion stack' — we entered it but haven't finished. Black means 'completely explored'. The distinction between grey and black is the whole trick: revisiting a *black* node is harmless (it's already placed), but reaching a *grey* node means we've walked an edge back to an ancestor on the current path — a **back edge**, which is the definition of a cycle in a directed graph.

**Why a plain visited boolean isn't enough.** A single 'visited' flag can't distinguish 'seen on this path' from 'seen on a previous, finished path'. Two separate DFS trees can legitimately share a node without any cycle. Only the grey state — 'still on the stack right now' — correctly flags a cycle. Conflating black with grey would report false cycles on diamond-shaped DAGs like example 2.

**Bailing out on a cycle.** The moment DFS hits a grey node we know the schedule is impossible, so we short-circuit all the way up and return an empty array. Otherwise, after every node is black, we reverse the post-order list and return it.
approaches.insight: Kahn's builds the order front-to-back from the sources; DFS builds it back-to-front from the sinks. They're two views of the same partial order. The grey/black split is the directed-graph analogue of 'am I revisiting myself or just an old neighbour?' — the question that separates a cycle from a harmless re-encounter.

edgeCases.behavior: Constraints forbid aᵢ == bᵢ, but if present, node 0's edge to itself hits a grey node → cycle → [].
The outer loop restarts DFS on each unvisited (white) node so every component is ordered.
dfs(0) finishes immediately; post-order [0] reversed is [0].

pitfalls: Using a single visited boolean instead of 3 colours — reports false cycles on diamond DAGs.
Forgetting to reverse the post-order list — yields the exact reverse of a valid order.
Not restarting DFS on every unvisited node — misses disconnected components.
Deep recursion on a long chain (up to 2000 nodes) — usually fine, but Kahn's avoids the stack entirely.

commonMistakes: Building the graph with the edge direction reversed, producing a backwards order.
Seeding Kahn's queue with only course 0 rather than all zero-in-degree courses.
Returning a partial ordering when a cycle exists instead of an empty array.
Using a single visited flag in the DFS version, which misreports cycles on valid DAGs.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Reversing the prerequisite edge direction
commonMistakesDetailed.why: [a, b] means b is a prerequisite of a, so the edge must run b → a. Building a → b produces a topological order of the reversed graph — every prerequisite ends up AFTER the course that needs it.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning a partial order on a cycle
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When a cycle exists, Kahn's schedules only the acyclic part, so the output is shorter than numCourses. Returning it ignores the impossibility; the spec requires an empty array.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Single visited flag in DFS misdetects cycles
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A boolean 'visited' can't tell 'on the current recursion stack' from 'finished on an earlier path'. Two DFS trees can share a node legitimately; only the grey state flags a real back edge.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
state = [0] * n  # 0=white, 1=grey, 2=black
def dfs(u):
    state[u] = 1
    for v in adj[u]:
        if state[v] == 1: return False        # back edge = cycle
        if state[v] == 0 and not dfs(v): return False
    state[u] = 2
    return True

followupVariations.hint: Peel leaves layer by layer (an undirected analogue of Kahn's) until 1–2 centroid nodes remain.

patternNote: Topological sort of a DAG. Kahn's BFS peels zero-in-degree sources and detects cycles by a short output; DFS post-order reversal does it from the sinks with 3-colour cycle detection. Same family as Course Schedule I, Alien Dictionary, Parallel Courses, and build-dependency ordering.
